page7_img_1.png.title: Top-ranked ML engineering challenges by practitioner experience
page7_img_1.png.description: A table comparing which ML engineering challenges respondents reported most often, showing percentage changes in frequency (Medium vs. Low and High vs. Low experience) and the rank of each challenge within Low/Medium/High experience buckets. 'Data Availability, Collection, Cleaning, and Management' is ranked #1 for all experience groups and shows a −2% change for medium but a large +60% increase for high-experience respondents, indicating it remains a dominant concern as teams mature. 'Education and Training' is highly important to low-experience respondents (rank 1) but drops substantially for medium and high experience (−69% and −78% respectively; ranks 5 and 9). In contrast, items like 'AI Tools', 'Scale', and 'Model Evolution, Evaluation, and Deployment' show large positive frequency changes (e.g., Model Evolution +137% medium, +276% high) and move up in rank for more experienced practitioners, reflecting that tooling, scalability, and model lifecycle issues become more salient with greater AI experience.

page8_img_1.png.title: Average Overall Effectiveness (OE) of ML Practices by Application Domain
page8_img_1.png.description: A horizontal dot‑plot showing anonymized application domains labeled A through I on the x‑axis and each domain’s mean Overall Effectiveness (OE) plotted as a single dot (y‑axis labels are elided for confidentiality). Domains A–F are plotted as black dots and are generally higher on the y‑axis (A being the highest, then B and C, followed by D–F), while domains G–I are plotted as red dots and lie noticeably lower. Dashed horizontal grid lines emphasize the vertical separation and an ANOVA with a Scott–Knott test grouped the domains into two statistically distinct clusters (black: A–F; red: G–I), indicating the OE metric differentiates maturity across domains.

page2_img_1.png.title: Nine-stage machine learning workflow with iterative feedback
page2_img_1.png.description: A left-to-right schematic of the nine stages used to build ML systems: Model Requirements → Data Collection → Data Cleaning → Data Labeling → Feature Engineering → Model Training → Model Evaluation → Model Deployment → Model Monitoring. The three early stages (collection, cleaning, labeling) show database icons emphasizing their data-centric role, while gears and other small icons mark stages where engineering/automation is important (e.g., feature engineering, training, deployment). Two kinds of feedback are depicted: a small curved arrow from Model Training back to Feature Engineering (e.g., representation learning) and larger curved arrows from Model Evaluation and Model Monitoring that can loop back to any prior stage, illustrating the iterative, non-linear nature of model development and maintenance.

page4_img_table_1.png.title: Table of interviewed stakeholders by role, product area, and manager status
page4_img_table_1.png.description: A four-column table enumerating 14 interviewees (IDs I1–I14) with columns: Id, Role, Product Area, and Manager?. The first nine rows (I1–I9) are marked "Yes" for Manager and the last five (I10–I14) are marked "No." Listed roles include Applied Scientist (I1–I2), Architect, Engineering/General Manager, multiple Program Managers, Researcher/Scientist, and several Software Engineers; product areas cover Search, Conversation, Vision, ML Tools, Productivity Tools, Speech, AI Platform, Community, and Ads. The table illustrates that the interview sample was largely senior and cross-functional across core ML product domains, consistent with the paper’s note that interviewees were largely in senior leadership roles.
